title: Stand the night
hook: O you wrapped in garments, stand in the night, except a little (73:1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: masjid, the mosques are for Allah, and your line, the mosque is his. Did an ordinary spot look like a place of prayer? Today, a new surah, and a call that comes in the dark. Day six hundred fifty-two.

It's the middle of the night. The house is asleep. You're under a heavy blanket, pulled up to your chin, the warmest you've been all day. And someone speaks to you, gently, by the name of what you're doing. You, wrapped up. Get up. Not all night. Most of it, or half, or a little less. That is how surah seventy-three begins. It's addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and it calls him by his blanket: al-muzzammil, the one wrapped up.

Verses one and two, in Pickthall's translation: "O thou wrapped up in thy raiment! Keep vigil the night long, save a little." Then verses three and four make it flexible: half the night, or a little less, or a little more. Some commentators hear the name as tender: not a formal title but a description, almost a nickname. They note that Arabs sometimes addressed someone by what they were doing at that moment, as a kind of affection. Some connect the wrapping to the beginning of revelation. Sahih al-Bukhari tells how, after the first revelation in the cave of Hira, the Prophet came home shaking and said to his wife Khadijah: wrap me, wrap me. Commentators differ on whether this surah came right after that, but it is counted among the early ones. And then the call: stand. Qiyam al-layl, standing the night in prayer. Verse six explains why: rising by night is stronger for the heart and more fitting for words. The night is quieter. Nobody's watching. Your phone, ideally, is face down. Words said at two in the morning tend to be meant. Verse five gives another reason: We are about to send down on you a weighty word. Before the heavy work of carrying the message in daylight, the Prophet was given the training of the night. Today this practice is often called tahajjud, voluntary prayer after sleep, in the last part of the night. Some do it every night, some during Ramadan, some only now and then. The invitation of the surah is the same: get up from the blanket, and stand.

The practice: two units at night. If you pray, you can get up tonight, or before dawn, and pray two short units, two rak'ahs, even if it's only once this week. For now, sit as if it were the middle of the night. Lower the lights if you can. Let the house go quiet in your mind. Notice how different your attention feels when nobody needs anything from you. Stay in that quiet. The bell holds the time.
Al-muzzammil. The one wrapped up: in 73:1–2 the Prophet, under his blanket, is called to rise and pray through the night, all but a little. Today's word.
Your line: stand in the night. Tonight, set an alarm a little before dawn, or simply sit up for two minutes before sleep, and spend them in quiet prayer or stillness. Day six hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Some Muslims pray tahajjud, voluntary night prayer in units of two rak'ahs, after sleeping and before dawn; some keep it nightly, others mostly in Ramadan or now and then, following the call of al-Muzzammil and the Prophet's practice.

fork.setup: you're wrapped in a warm blanket in the middle of the night. the call comes: stand. how much of the night does 73:2–4 ask for?
options: half, a bit less, or a bit more.
fork.reveal: all night except a little: half, a little less, or a little more. the call is flexible, and gentle.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'many commentators/scholars/Muslims' claims softened to 'some'; the practice now offers night prayer with 'if you pray, you can' instead of 'you're invited'; the myth reveal attributes the nickname reading to commentators; 'whatever you say you mean' no longer tells the listener what they mean.
Pickthall wording of 73:1–2 quoted from memory; please confirm.
Bukhari 3 records 'zammiluni' (wrap me) after Hira; the link of this surah to that moment is debated among commentators, which the script says.
The claim that addressing someone by their current state was a sign of affection follows tafsir (e.g. on 'ya muzzammil'); confirm.
Tahajjud defined as voluntary night prayer after sleep; confirm wording.

Reviewer softened the teach: 'the name is tender, not a title of honor' was stated as settled; it is now attributed to commentators, since some read al-muzzammil as an honorific address. Note also that the 'wrap me' (zammiluni/daththiruni) narrations are linked by many to al-Muddaththir (74) as much as to al-Muzzammil.
